(1) for a given time baseline, a large number of observations is more effective than a small number of long-duration observations, and (2) there is no observational noise floor.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, to detect a planet in a 10-year orbit around a 1 M _{☉} star with a 5% radial-velocity amplitude, one needs 10 observations spread over at least a year.
the most efficient way of detecting Jupiter-like planets is to maximize the time baseline and to minimize the time span of the observations, rather than increasing the number of observations.
the most important observational strategy for the detection of Jupiter-like planets is to obtain a large number of measurements over a long time baseline.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to detect a Jupiter analog in a given system, one needs to obtain a minimum of N observations over a time span of at least one orbital period.
a large number of observations with modest time coverage can be as effective as a smaller number of observations with a longer time coverage.

the number of observations needed to achieve a given detection limit is not proportional to the number of orbital periods sampled but rather to the square root of N, which can be as small as 1/10 the total number of orbital periods.
